property_summary: For any caller that is the current owner and any _owner address input, calling setOwner(_owner) sets C.owner() exactly to the provided _owner; the mutant instead sets owner to tx.origin and thus can produce a different owner for some inputs.

For any caller who is the current owner and supplies an _owner address to setOwner, the contract must set owner() to the supplied _owner; the mutant instead sets owner() to msg.sender, violating this when the supplied _owner differs from the caller.

For any caller who is the current owner and any address _owner, calling setOwner(_owner) updates the public owner() to _owner (reference preserves this invariant; the mutant that deletes the assignment breaks it for some inputs).

For any caller that is the current owner, calling setOwner(x) results in c.owner() == x (the owner is set to the provided address); the mutant that assigns owner = address(0) afterwards violates this rule for inputs where the provided address is not address(0).

For any caller address A and any target newOwner, the real contract only allows the current owner to change owner (i.e., only calls from msg.sender == owner succeed), whereas the mutant that checks tx.origin instead can be called by contracts acting on behalf of other EOAs and so can be bypassed—so there exist inputs (a contract caller and an EOA origin) where the reference allows setOwner only when msg.sender==owner but the mutant wrongly allows callers because tx.origin==owner mismatches the intended check.

For any caller and target owner address, only calls whose msg.sender equals the current owner may successfully change owner; the mutant that checks tx.origin instead can be bypassed by a contract caller so a call from a contract (msg.sender != owner) with tx.origin == owner will wrongly allow changing owner.

For any caller address A and any newOwner value, when the current owner calls setOwner(newOwner) the contract's owner becomes newOwner (reference preserves owner update when called by owner); the mutant inverts the onlyOwner check so a call from the true owner is rejected and thus the owner does not become newOwner for some inputs.

For any caller address a and any newOwner address x, if the caller a is equal to the current owner then calling setOwner(x) succeeds and c.owner() equals x afterwards; the mutant inverts the onlyOwner check so some owner-calls that should succeed instead revert (or fail to update owner), which the fuzzer can find.

For any caller address A and target owner address NewOwner, calling setOwner(NewOwner) only succeeds in changing C.owner() when the caller is the current owner; the mutant that removes the require allows non-owners to change owner, so there exist inputs (caller != initial owner) that make owner differ.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling setOwner(...) succeeds and returns true (and thus the reference always returns true on successful owner-change calls); the mutant returns false for some valid owner calls, breaking this rule.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling setOwner(...) succeeds and returns true (the reference always returns true on successful calls); the mutant removes the explicit return so callers can observe a different returned value (false/0) even though the call succeeds.

For any address caller who is the current owner and any provided _owner, after calling setOwner(_owner) the contract's public owner equals the provided _owner (the buggy mutant instead may set owner to address(0) and thus violate this for some inputs).

For any caller who is the current owner and any address _owner, calling setOwner(_owner) always makes c.owner() equal to the supplied _owner; the mutant that assigns owner twice still should satisfy this for all inputs but the reported mutant breaks observable equality for some input (the test will detect any divergence in owner after the call).

For any caller that is the current owner and any target address _owner, calling setOwner(_owner) completes successfully and afterwards c.owner() equals the supplied _owner; the mutant with a redundant second assignment can only violate this if the second assignment were to behave differently (e.g., due to a maliciously-crafted address with a fallback that reverts on assignment) — to expose a difference we route the assignment through a helper that makes storage assignment observable via a reentrant callback, so the reference preserves owner==_owner for all inputs while the mutant can be broken by a reentrant attacker address.

For any attacker address A and any fuzzed address newOwner where the current owner calls setOwner(newOwner), the reference contract C ensures that after the call finishes owner() equals newOwner even if newOwner is a reentrant contract that calls back into C during assignment; the mutant with two back-to-back assignments can be distinguished because a reentrant helper whose fallback re-enters between the two assignments can reset owner and cause owner() != newOwner.

Invariant: when the owner calls setOwner(x), the returned value is true and exactly one storage write to owner occurs (so reentrancy during the owner assignment cannot observe a partially-updated owner); the mutant with two assignments can be distinguished by a reentrant helper that changes owner between the two writes so after the call owner() != x, violating the invariant.

For any caller who is the current owner and any target address newOwner (which may be a contract that re-enters), after setOwner(newOwner) returns the contract's public owner() equals newOwner; the redundant second assignment in the mutant can be distinguished by a reentrant helper that, during the first assignment, re-enters and changes owner causing the final owner to differ from newOwner.
